For radical feminists, this biological truth is the foundation of our analysis of patriarchy. Our oppression as females is not based on “gender identity”; it is based on our biological sex. The Erasure of Sex: A Radical Feminist Case for Biological Reality and Women's Boundaries

Introduction

I. The Biological Foundation of Womanhood

Sex Is Binary, Observable, and Immutable

Human beings, like all mammals, are a sexually dimorphic species. Sex is determined at fertilization by chromosomal composition — XX in females, XY in males — and is subsequently organized around the production of one of two gamete types: ova (large gametes) or sperm (small gametes). This binary is not a social construct, a spectrum, or a matter of assignment. It is a fundamental biological reality observed across virtually all complex animal life on earth.

From this chromosomal blueprint emerges a cascade of developmental consequences: hormonal profiles, reproductive anatomy, skeletal structure, musculature, organ function, and patterns of disease susceptibility. A male human who undergoes cross-sex hormone therapy and surgical modification does not thereby become female. He acquires a modified male body. His cells remain XY. His bones retain male skeletal dimensions. His prostate remains. His pattern of disease risk, while altered by exogenous hormones, does not replicate the female pattern. Medicine increasingly recognizes the danger of ignoring sex-based differences in treatment — a recognition that is directly undermined by the conflation of sex with gender identity.

The existence of intersex conditions — disorders of sexual development (DSDs) — is frequently invoked to argue that sex is a spectrum. This is a misuse of developmental pathology. Intersex conditions are precisely that: disorders of a binary system, not evidence that the binary does not exist. The existence of people born with fewer or more than ten fingers does not call into question whether humans are a ten-fingered species. DSDs are extremely rare, clinically identifiable deviations from the norm, and the overwhelming majority of transgender-identified individuals are not intersex. They have entirely typical male or female biology.

The concept of gender identity — an internal, subjective sense of being a man, a woman, or something else — has no reliable biomarker, no diagnostic test, and no falsifiability criterion. It is a metaphysical claim about the nature of the self, not a material reality subject to empirical verification. When proponents assert that "trans women are women," they are making a definitional claim that substitutes subjective feeling for objective observation. No rigorous scientific study has identified a mechanism by which a male brain can be "female" or vice versa. Radical feminism insists on the primacy of material reality. Women are not women because they feel like women. They are women because they were born into the sex class that gestates, lactates, and menstruates — or that possesses the developmental organization oriented toward those functions, even when individual variation or medical conditions prevent their expression. A post-menopausal woman is still female. A woman who has undergone a hysterectomy is still female. Their femaleness is a fact of developmental biology, not contingent on current function.

Arguing for the maintenance of sex-based categories is not a call for cruelty. The redefinition of "woman" to include any person who claims the identity is not a minor semantic adjustment. It is a political revolution that strikes at the foundation of feminist thought, dismantles the legal and material protections women have built over generations, and demands that women accept male-bodied individuals into their most intimate and vulnerable spaces on pain of social, professional, and legal punishment.
